title: Two Sizes Up
passage:
Trevor Hoskadale went up two mesh sizes in his cod end – the tail of the trawl – and waited for the small haddock to see themselves out. They did not. A whole spring on, the boxes at the harbour looked much as they had the year before.

“A net is one thing on the deck and another thing down there,” he says. “Tow it, and every mesh pulls long and thin. The hole you measured with your hand is a slot by then. A haddock is round, and it has to get its width through.”

The second change was to the hanging, not the size. He had the same twine turned right round the bag, so the meshes stood as open squares under the drag. The small haddock went out. The plaice were much as before, a flat fish and a stretched mesh being much the same shape. He had not bargained for good fish going out too, on the tows when the square bars ran slack.

– Alison Hebden, gear pages

questions.prompt: What is said about the cod end Hoskadale tows?

options.text: The two extra mesh sizes did what he expected and let the small haddock out.
The plaice left the bag as readily as the haddock once the meshes were turned.
The gain came from a panel of square netting set into the top of the bag.
Towing closed the meshes, so the extra size did not give a round fish its width.

questions.rationale: KEY D paraphrases the load-bearing pair of claims the passage actually makes: the mesh sizes went up and nothing changed (“They did not. A whole spring on, the boxes at the harbour looked much as they had the year before.”), and the skipper's own explanation of why (“Tow it, and every mesh pulls long and thin. The hole you measured with your hand is a slot by then. A haddock is round, and it has to get its width through.”). A stretched mesh keeps its length and loses its width, so a bigger diamond does not hand a round-bodied fish the dimension it needs. No wording is lifted: the passage never uses “closed”, “extra size” or “give ... its width” in that arrangement. A is the quantifier-free version of the received rule (bigger mesh, more escapes) glued onto the passage's own opening move: the passage does say he went up two sizes, and a reader who stops at the first sentence supplies the expected outcome themselves. It is refuted by three words – “They did not.” – which is why it works as a skim-trap rather than a coin-flip. B is the true-statement-with-the-actor-swapped trap: the release of the small haddock after the turn is real (“The small haddock went out”), and B transplants it onto the plaice, whom the passage explicitly leaves unchanged (“The plaice were much as before”) and for a stated reason – a flat fish and a stretched mesh are much the same shape, so the old diamond mesh had never been the obstacle for them. C is the outside-knowledge trap sharpened with surface word-match: a square-mesh panel let into the top sheet is a real and very common escape device, so a solver with any gear knowledge finds it more plausible than the text does, and the word “squares” is in the passage to make it feel anchored. The passage rules it out: the change was to the hanging, not to an insert, and it was “the same twine turned right round the bag” – the whole cod end re-hung, not a panel set into part of it. None of A, B or C is true as written, so “best fit” is not doing any work here; each fails against a span a careful reader can point at.

generator_meta.genre: science_journalism (trade reportage from a fishing quay)
generator_meta.topic: why a trawl skipper's first fix failed and his second worked: going up two mesh sizes in a diamond-mesh cod end did not release the undersized haddock, because a diamond mesh elongates along the tow axis under the drag and loses lateral opening, and a round-bodied fish needs width, not length; re-hanging the same netting so the meshes stand as squares holds the opening under load and lets the small round fish out; the plaice are unaffected, because a flatfish cross-section already matches a stretched diamond; and the square hanging carries its own cost, since the transverse bars can go slack and let marketable fish out too

generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: GEAR-TECHNOLOGY CHECK, run 2026-09-01 BEFORE the passage was written, because a backwards mechanism is a V-FINAL kill and the batch15 TYPE-001 short was refuted on exactly that. Instruments: WebSearch until its session budget was exhausted, then Exa web search; every claim below is attached to the source that carries it. (1) DIAMOND MESH CLOSES UNDER TOW. Sala, Herrmann, De Carlo, Lucchetti & Brčić, 'Effect of Codend Circumference on the Size Selection of Square-Mesh Codends in Trawl Fisheries', PLOS ONE 11(7) e0160354 (2016): 'When the diamond-mesh codend is towed through the sea, the drag forces acting on the catch in the aft portion of the codend tend to stretch the meshes in most codend areas, causing a reduction in the opening angle. Only a few rows of diamond meshes, just in front of the catch accumulating in the codend, provide an opening angle wide enough for the escapement of round fish species.' Depestele, Polet, Van Craeynest & Vandendriessche, 'An overview of sea trials with the alternative beam trawl' (ILVO/vliz.be, 2011), citing Stewart & Robinson (1985) and Wileman et al. (1996): 'Diamond meshes have the tendency to close when they are stretched... All meshes in front of this zone are stretched and have a reduced mesh opening. The number of meshes through which fish can escape is thus seriously reduced.' This is the passage's 'every mesh pulls long and thin' and 'The hole you measured with your hand is a slot by then'. (2) SQUARE HANGING HOLDS THE OPENING, AND IT IS THE ROUND FISH THAT BENEFIT. Bak-Jensen, Herrmann & Santos, 'The capability of square-meshes and fixed-shape meshes to control codend size selection' (literatur.thuenen.de/digbib_extern/dn066269.pdf), citing Robertson & Stewart (1988): square-mesh codends have 'bars that are parallel to both transversal... and the longitudinal direction', and 'the parallel bars should keep the meshes more uniform and open as the tension from the drag forces in the mesh bars does not close the meshes which is not the case for diamond meshes'. Seafish fishing-gear database, 'Square Mesh Cod-ends': 'As the mesh size and shape stays constant, square mesh cod-ends are very efficient at allowing the easy release of small round fish, whilst retaining the larger fish... The square shape of the mesh better suits the cross sectional shape of the round fish for escape through the meshes than the shape of flat fish.' This is 'the same twine turned right round the bag, so the meshes stood as open squares under the drag. The small haddock went out.' (3) SAME OR EVEN LARGER DIAMOND MESH IS NOT ENOUGH - the premise of the whole unit. Conservation Evidence / T90 literature summarised in the same search: 'square meshes are found to maintain their shapes during towing and are hence found to be more selective than diamond mesh codend with same or even larger mesh sizes'; and Bak-Jensen et al. on mesh-openness variability: 'This variability in openness can negate the effect of gear modifications to reduce unwanted catches, such as increasing mesh size. Thereby, it can be questioned how well mesh size works as a regulating tool for management.' Quantitatively, the turned-mesh comparison in the same body of work gives whiting L50 26 cm turned against 12 cm standard. This licenses the passage's central non-result: two sizes up, and the boxes looked the same. (4) THE PLAICE. Depestele et al. (2011), citing Fonteyne & M'Rabet (1992) and Walsh et al. (1992): 'square meshes are less selective for flatfish compared to diamond meshes. The rationale behind it was that diamond meshes have a shape similar to the body shape of flatfish, thus allowing an easier passage through the mesh compared to the square mesh.' Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries (2025), 'Understanding and predicting codend size selection for flatfish species': 'The morphology of flatfish is compressed and asymmetrical... This morphology has often been associated with having good escape properties from elongated diamond meshes in the codend compared to square meshes.' And, decisively for the passage's exact wording, the trade source reports the skipper-level observation verbatim in substance - Seafish, 'Square Mesh Cod-ends': 'Many skippers have reported that they have seen no difference in the retained catch of flat fish when they have fitted a square mesh cod-end of a similar mesh size to their original diamond mesh, but have managed to release in the region of 90% of the small round fish.' This is 'The plaice were much as before, a flat fish and a stretched mesh being much the same shape.' (5) THE RESIDUE, which is the passage's closing detail and is NOT what any option turns on. Bak-Jensen et al., reporting Krag et al. (2011) and Herrmann et al. (2016): 'the tension in the bars in square-mesh is mainly in longitudinal, while the two remaining bars (transversal) may well be slack and deformable. This can result in larger fish being able to escape through square-meshes than desirable, increasing the variability in size selection.' This is 'He had not bargained for good fish going out too, on the tows when the square bars ran slack.' (6) A REJECTED DISTRACTOR, logged because it was rejected on physics and not on taste. An earlier draft used 'a thicker twine... held the meshes apart against the drag' as the outside-knowledge distractor. The literature runs the other way - Lowry & Robertson, 'The effect of twine thickness on cod-end selectivity of trawls for haddock in the North Sea', Fisheries Research 26 (1996); Kynoch & Zuur (1999); O'Neill & Herrmann on PRESEMO - thicker and stiffer twine REDUCES lateral mesh opening and lowers L50. Since the distractor would have been backwards as world fact rather than merely absent from the text, it was replaced by the square-mesh-panel distractor (C), which is world-TRUE and passage-false, which is the trap shape TYPE-001 actually wants. (7) NOT VERIFIED: no ICES working-group report, no EU technical measures regulation and no flume-tank study was read in full; the evidence is the passages quoted above from a peer-reviewed PLOS ONE paper, a Thünen-Institut preprint, a 2025 Springer review, an ILVO sea-trials report and the Seafish gear database. Mesh sizes are deliberately unnumbered in the passage ('two mesh sizes'), so the unit asserts no specific millimetre figure and no jurisdiction's legal minimum.
